## The dataset, and what makes our variant special

DrivAerML is 484 parametrically morphed DrivAer notchback variants with
time-averaged fields from scale-resolving CFD — surface pressure and
wall shear on ~8.8M-point vehicle surfaces, plus volume fields. It is
"steady" in the statistically-stationary sense of the RANS charter:
the labels are time averages of a turbulent flow, which is exactly the
setting the program's scope was written for (the closure is empirical;
the equations are not given).

The variant used here (the internal BC-labeled curation) differs from
the public distribution in the one way this program cares about most:
**every case carries the actual boundary-value problem.** Five named,
BC-typed boundary meshes — the `vehicle`, a `no_slip` ground plane
beginning just ahead of the car, `slip` tunnel walls and ceiling, an
`inlet`, and an `outlet` — plus per-case freestream values
($U_\infty$, $p_\infty$, $\rho_\infty$, $\nu$, $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$) as
global data. The public release includes only the vehicle geometry, which
is the interesting *shape* but not the posed *problem*.

## The standing hypothesis

Every model currently wired into the unified external-aero recipe
consumes only the vehicle surface; the other four labeled boundaries
sit in the data unused. The `MeshTransformer`'s typed-boundary schema
consumes all five natively — and the mixed-BC discriminator suite
(@sec-mixed-bc) measured exactly this setting as one where attention
matters.

- **H-ground (the headline experiment).** Feeding all five typed
  boundaries beats the vehicle-only formulation on surface pressure
  near the underbody and wake, because ground effect is real physics
  that the vehicle-only formulation must hallucinate from shape priors.
  *Falsifier: five-boundary arm no better than vehicle-only at matched
  budget and matched sampling — which would mean the fixed far
  boundaries are adequately encoded in the freestream vector alone,
  itself a publishable negative.*

## Integration plan

The recipe is `DomainMesh`-native and registry-free: a new model is one
YAML under `conf/model/` declaring `forward_kwargs` resolved from
DomainMesh paths. The `MeshTransformer` enters as a mesh-native model
(the same pattern the in-tree GLOBE configs use), with two arms:

1. `mesh_transformer_vehicle` — `boundaries.vehicle` only, matching
   every existing model's information diet (the fair-comparison arm);
2. `mesh_transformer_allbc` — all five typed boundaries (the
   H-ground arm).

Surface task first (pressure + wall shear at surface centroids;
force-coefficient integration comes free from the recipe's inference
path), volume task second. Training at the recipe's sampling
resolution (50k–200k surface points, batch 1) requires the
checkpointed decode — the wall and its fix are @sec-scale's story,
whose paired B200 measurement accompanies this campaign.

## Results {#sec-drivaerml-results}

Two campaigns resolved here. The first answered the chapter's
pre-registered question (H-ground) — with its falsifier, in the
neutral form. The second was not planned in this chapter at all: a
40× deficit against the recipe's GeoTransolver baseline triggered a
root-cause investigation (@sec-nb-geot-gap) whose constructive
output — the boundary-trace mode plus two protocol findings, and the
capacity rungs they unlocked — ultimately moved the program's
DrivAerML floor by 14.5× with a per-step mechanism attribution (the
ledger below).

### H-ground: a neutral result

Three arms at matched 500-epoch, 4-node protocol (1 seed/arm;
provenance `output/drivaer_v2/*.log`, HSG): vehicle-only val
**0.1019**, all-five-boundaries **0.1026**, per-boundary-pooled
**0.1036**. The pre-registered falsifier fires in its neutral form
(@sec-nb-hground-verdict): with the vehicle-starvation and
drive-overflow confounds fixed, the four labeled tunnel boundaries
neither help nor hurt. At 722 panels for an entire ground plane, the
far boundaries carry little exploitable signal beyond what the
freestream vector already encodes — **for surface-field prediction at
this resolution, the boundary-value problem's far boundaries are
adequately encoded in the freestream.** A publishable negative, per
the pre-registration; caveats attached: single seed per arm, no
banded underbody/wake decomposition.

Two pipeline findings from this campaign outlived it (both
upstreamed): the reader's dual-cap subsampling starved the vehicle to
378 cells (fixed by the topology-aware reader, PR #1819), and the
norm-free drive stream overflows on raw dimensional freestreams
(fixed by unit-direction encoding — a model *lesson*, not a bug: the
zero-preserving stream is norm-free by design, so its inputs must
arrive nondimensionalized).

### The gap investigation and the trace mechanism

Every capacity variant at the v2 protocol crowded into one band —
plain 0.1019, members 0.0999, wide 0.0990, allbc/pooled 0.102–0.104 —
while GeoTransolver reached 0.061 after *one epoch* under the
identical trainer. The investigation (@sec-nb-geot-gap-verdict)
killed the metric and data hypotheses and isolated two mechanisms:
a representational floor specific to on-boundary queries (H-D), and
a representational-efficiency gap (H-C).

H-D's constructive fix is the **boundary-trace mode**: surface
queries sit exactly on the double layer's jump discontinuity, and the
closed form serves the *interior* limit (−½) where the physics needs
the *exterior* trace (+½). Declaring the query mesh to be the
boundary licenses the exact one-sided correction plus own-cell typed
read-outs (@sec-nb-trace-mode). Verdict at protocol end
(@sec-nb-trace-verdict): **the pre-registered ≥5× acceptance is
REFUTED — measured 2.03×** (0.1019 → 0.0503) — but trace is the only
intervention that ever broke the 0.10 plateau, and the corrected arm
then plateaus again at ~0.049. The floor moved, and stopped: the
signature of the *next* representational ceiling, owned by H-C.
(The 2.03× is trace's effect at the small pre-ladder configuration;
the completed factorial later measured **3.8× at flagship
capacity** — mechanisms scale individually, and this one grew.
@sec-drivaerml-trace-factorial.)

### The capacity ladder, post-trace (T2)

With the trace floor removed, does capacity buy accuracy again?
Matched 1-node protocol on GB300 (single seed per rung — the
pre-registered ladder design; provenance `output/drivaer_t2/*.log`,
AGA):

| rung | final val (ep500) | vs trace |
|---|---|---|
| trace (reference dims) | 0.0288 | — |
| trace + ranks 2× | 0.0284 | +1.4% (noise) |
| **trace + operator_layers 2** | **0.0228** | **+26%** |

The ladder is *selectively* ordered (@sec-nb-t2-verdict): encoder
**depth** improves validation error by 26%; attention **rank** has no
measured effect. The
post-trace floor is limited by the compositional depth of boundary
processing, not the width of the attention bottleneck. The depth
rung's single-seed caveat is resolved: 3-seed finals
0.0228/0.0224/0.0212 (@sec-nb-probes-verdict) — tight spread, the
+26% holds.

### The effective-batch windfall

The ladder's cross-cluster control produced its own finding: the
*identical* trace configuration reads **0.0288 at 1-node** (108
optimizer steps/epoch) vs **0.0503 at the 16-GPU protocol** (27
steps/epoch) — 1.75× better from effective batch size alone, at a
500-epoch budget. Consequence, flagged wherever numbers cross
protocols: **no cross-protocol comparison in this chapter is valid
without a matched-batch control**, including against the
GeoTransolver anchor — hence the matched 1-node control in the next
section.

The windfall's converse later closed the multi-node question
(@sec-nb-mn-verdict): 4-node DDP at matched LR and the same
500-epoch budget pays **1.58× (flagship), 1.56× (×2), ~2.2× (×4)**
against its 1-node twin — the effective-batch penalty does not
shrink with model scale. Multi-node reduces wall-clock for inference
and production retrains; ladder rungs stay 1-node.

The mechanism itself was then isolated by the pre-registered 2×2
(@sec-nb-b22-verdict): a 16-GPU arm run for 2000 epochs — matching
the 1-node arm's optimizer-update count — finals at 0.0212
(2 seeds), against 0.0221 for the 500-epoch 16-GPU arm and 0.0140
for 1-node. Quadrupling the updates at large batch recovers only
~11% of the small-batch advantage: **the effective-batch effect is
the gradient noise (small-batch regularization) itself, not
optimizer-step count.** Held equal within the 16-GPU column:
configuration, learning rate, schedule shape, and data; the
1-node column's schedule differs by its queries-per-step scaling,
by design of the original comparison — the clean isolation is the
16-GPU column, and it is decisive.

### The ledger

$$
\underbrace{0.1019}_{\text{v2 protocol}}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{exterior trace (exact)}}\;
\underbrace{0.0503}_{2.03\times}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{effective batch}}\;
\underbrace{0.0288}_{1.75\times}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{encoder depth}}\;
\underbrace{0.0224}_{1.29\times}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{composition}}\;
\underbrace{0.0140}_{1.60\times}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{scale}\ (\times 2\ \text{dims})}\;
\underbrace{0.0093}_{1.51\times}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{scale}\ (\times\ \text{depth})}\;
\underbrace{0.00702}_{1.32\times}
$$

**Fourteen-and-a-half-fold, in six named steps** — jump relation,
optimization steps, compositional depth, mechanism composition, and
parameters along two confirmed axes — each a licensed, understood
mechanism, not a tuning outcome (depth is the 3-seed value; the
composition and scale steps are detailed in the sections below). The
distance to GeoTransolver is quoted only against the
matched-protocol control (next section).

### The matched GeoTransolver control, and where the gap lives

The 1-node GeoTransolver control finished at **0.00249** (ep499) —
within 2% of its 16-GPU anchor, so GeoTransolver gains nothing from
the batch effect that gave us 1.75×. Against the ledger's endpoint:
**2.8× at the ×2L4 rung** (0.00702), down from 40× at the start
of the investigation — and the scale-law section below turns that
single ratio into a curve. Per-epoch wall-clock is comparable between the
models at this protocol; what the sections below decompose is *where*
the remaining distance lives (@sec-nb-tail-verdict,
@sec-nb-t3-launch).

The efficiency probes locate it further — and then, on the strongest
base, exclude the leading suspect. **P1** (optimizer): refuted by
inspection — both models share the trainer's exact settings. **P2**
(local-geometry diagnostic; contract-breaking by design and never a
candidate for retention): CONFIRMED for efficiency *on the singpair-trace base* —
persistently ~100 epochs ahead at equal quality — but only +7% at
the converged floor. **P3** (supervision density): ¼-density costs
~35% at protocol end. That P2 signature motivated a declared local
corrector (classical BIE-style near-field structure in the decoder),
gated on a pre-registered probe ladder — and **the probes returned a
triple null** (@sec-nb-probes-verdict). On the deep2+members base,
the same local information — entering through the decode kernel (A),
restricted to a subtended-angle near field (B), or replaced by a
matched-width global latent (C) — moves neither the efficiency curve
nor the floor:

| arm (seed 43) | ep25 | ep50 | ep100 | ep~300 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| control (deep2+members) | 0.0487 | 0.0341 | 0.0234 | 0.0213 |
| A: kernel-side local | 0.0488 | 0.0352 | 0.0247 | 0.0226 |
| B: near-field only | 0.0467 | 0.0347 | 0.0244 | 0.0225 |
| C: global-latent control | 0.0461 | 0.0355 | 0.0246 | 0.0227 |

Synthesis: **local-geometry information is subsumed by
depth+members capacity** — the strong base learns whatever those
features encode quickly on its own (the same subsumption pattern as
the AirFRANS pseudo-composition result, one level up). The corrector
is a **no-go**: its premise was refuted in a two-GPU-day probe instead of a
multi-day build. GeoTransolver's ~25× epoch-efficiency advantage
persists with local shortcuts now *excluded* as its mechanism on
strong bases; the round-2 probes below take up the remaining
suspects — and find that the boring one carries.

### The factorial, and the composition story

The members × trace factorial completed at the 16-GPU protocol
(anchors: plain 0.1019, trace 0.0503, members 0.0999;
@sec-nb-factorial-verdict):

| arm | final val | vs trace |
|---|---|---|
| members + trace | 0.0458 | 1.10× |
| **members + wide + trace** | **0.0270** | **1.86×** |

Members at reference width remains a near-null even post-trace
(+10%, echoing its +2% pre-trace). But trace and **width** compose
*super*-multiplicatively: trace bought 2.03× on the plain arm and
**3.7×** on the wide arm — width was starved *behind* the trace
defect. This is the interaction the flagship arm banks on.

### The flagship: composition confirmed

The all-mechanism composition — trace × members × wide ×
operator_layers 2, 1-node protocol — finished at
**0.0138/0.0140/0.0156** across its three seeds
(@sec-nb-flagship-verdict): every seed under the pre-registered
≤0.020 acceptance. Against the 3-seed depth rung (0.0224) the
composition adds another 1.60× — the mechanisms stack rather than
substitute, with the trace×width interaction carrying the load
exactly as the factorial predicted.

### H-C round 2: it's parameters, not rounds

With local shortcuts excluded, a structural diff of GeoTransolver's
source named the remaining suspects — per-point residual read-out,
learned soft-slice routing × 12 refinement rounds, LN-everywhere —
and one confound that round-1 discipline required excluding first:
**raw scale.** GeoTransolver runs ≈9.5M parameters; the flagship
≈0.6M — a 10–20× gap never tested (the early rank-doubling null was
rank-only, pre-trace, on the singpair base; the factorial had since
proven width×trace *super*-multiplicative). Two config-only ladders
on the flagship base answered both questions at once
(@sec-nb-hc2, @sec-nb-hc2-verdict):

| rung | params vs flagship | final val |
|---|---|---|
| flagship (×1) | 1× | 0.0140 (3-seed) |
| **scale: dims ×2** | ~4× | **0.0093 / 0.0095** (2 seeds) |
| scale: dims ×4 | ~16× | 0.0123 *at its stability LR/4 — see below* |
| iteration: 4 rounds, params matched | 1× | 0.0146 |
| iteration: 8 rounds, params matched | 1× | 0.0198 |
| iteration: 4 rounds, natural | ~2× | 0.0120 |
| iteration: 8 rounds, natural | ~4× | 0.0102 |

**The iterate-refine hypothesis is falsified at matched parameters**
— exchange-round count alone provides no benefit (4 rounds flat, 8 rounds
actively worse), and natural-depth gains track their parameter
growth. **Scale carries**: ×2 dims meets its pre-registered ≥1.3×
bar with margin. Two caveats. First, the ×4 rung froze at
initialization at the shared LR in both seeds (val 0.165 from ep1)
and trains only at LR/4 — a μP-style LR ∝ 1/width stability
constraint — where it finishes at **0.0123**, *worse* than ×2
despite 4× the parameters: **pure width bends under its own LR
constraint**, which is why the scale law below runs along the mixed
width×depth direction instead. Second, GeoTransolver's
epoch-efficiency edge *persists* (its ep-1 value still beats our ×2
arm's) — it just no longer implies a floor disadvantage. The rungs
PENDING at this round's close (further ×2 seeds and the
×2-dims-4-layer rung) are complete and are the next section's subject.

### A provisional LR-stable frontier, and where parity sits on it

How far does "scale carries" carry? The pre-registered fit
(@sec-nb-scalelaw-verdict) answers on a fixed protocol: 1-node, 500
epochs, **LR-stable rungs only** — the ×4 point is excluded as
optimization-constrained (the width bend above). Seed calibration
first: the ×2 rung's four runs span 0.0090–0.0114 (±12% about the
mean), so single-seed rungs carry that error bar and the fit uses
per-rung means.

| rung | params | val (ep500) |
|---|---|---|
| flagship | 0.6M | 0.0140 (3-seed) |
| + operator_layers 4 (L4) | 1.2M | 0.0120 |
| + operator_layers 8 (L8) | 2.4M | 0.0102 |
| dims ×2 | 2.4M | 0.00979 (4-run mean) |
| dims ×2 + L4 (×2L4) | 4.8M | **0.00702** |
| dims ×2 + L8 (×2L8) | 9.6M | **0.005828** |

The fit over all six rungs:
$\text{val} \approx 0.0125 \cdot P_{\mathrm{M}}^{-0.33}$, rms
log-residual 0.052 — globally still a line, but with a top-end
deviation: the newest doubling's local slope flattened to
0.27 (×2→×2L4 was 0.42), a **mild bend at the 9.6M rung**
(@sec-nb-x2l8-verdict).

```{python}
#| label: fig-scalelaw
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The parameter frontier on a fixed protocol (1 node, 500 epochs,
#|   LR-stable rungs only). Six rungs fit val = 0.0125 * P_M^-0.33 with
#|   rms log-residual 0.052. The x4 rung (hollow) is EXCLUDED from the
#|   fit: it froze at initialization at the shared learning rate and
#|   trains only at LR/4, where it finishes worse than x2 despite 4x the
#|   parameters -- pure width bending under a muP-style LR-proportional-
#|   to-1/width constraint. GeoTransolver's matched-protocol anchor sits
#|   2.34x below the curve at essentially the same budget; the dashed
#|   extension shows how far pure scaling would have to go to reach it,
#|   and the shaded fan is the difference between the global slope
#|   (0.33) and the flatter local slope of the newest doubling (0.27).
#|   The +/-12% band on the x2 rung is the measured 4-run seed spread and
#|   applies to every single-seed rung.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

### Rungs: (label, params in millions, val, LR-stable?)
rungs = [
    ("flagship", 0.6, 0.0140, True),
    ("L4", 1.2, 0.0120, True),
    ("L8", 2.4, 0.0102, True),
    ("×2", 2.4, 0.00979, True),
    ("×2L4", 4.8, 0.00702, True),
    ("×2L8", 9.6, 0.005828, True),
    ("×4", 9.6, 0.0123, False),
]
stable = [(p, v) for _, p, v, ok in rungs if ok]
params = np.array([p for p, _ in stable])
vals = np.array([v for _, v in stable])

### The chapter's pre-registered fit.
amplitude, slope = 0.0125, -0.33
local_slope = -0.27
incumbent_params, incumbent_val = 9.5, 0.00249

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.0))
grid = np.logspace(np.log10(0.5), np.log10(400), 200)
ax.plot(grid, amplitude * grid**slope, color="#2a78d6", lw=1.6,
        label="fit  $0.0125\\,P_\\mathrm{M}^{-0.33}$", zorder=2)

### How far pure scaling must go, under global vs local slope.
anchor_p, anchor_v = 9.6, 0.005828
far = grid[grid >= anchor_p]
ax.fill_between(far,
                anchor_v * (far / anchor_p) ** slope,
                anchor_v * (far / anchor_p) ** local_slope,
                color="#2a78d6", alpha=0.10, lw=0, zorder=1)
ax.plot(far, anchor_v * (far / anchor_p) ** local_slope, color="#2a78d6",
        lw=1.2, ls=":", zorder=2)

### Seed spread measured on the x2 rung, carried by every single-seed rung.
ax.errorbar(params, vals, yerr=vals * 0.12, fmt="none", ecolor="#898781",
            elinewidth=1.0, capsize=3, alpha=0.7, zorder=3)
ax.plot(params, vals, "o", ms=8, color="#2a78d6", mec="white", mew=1.2,
        zorder=4, label="LR-stable rungs (fitted)")
ax.plot(9.6, 0.0123, "o", ms=9, mfc="none", mec="#e34948", mew=1.8, zorder=4,
        label="×4 rung — LR-constrained, excluded")
ax.plot(incumbent_params, incumbent_val, "*", ms=17, color="#1baf7a",
        mec="white", mew=1.0, zorder=5, label="GeoTransolver (matched protocol)")

for label, p, v, ok in rungs:
    offset = (7, 5) if label != "×2" else (7, -13)
    ax.annotate(label, (p, v), textcoords="offset points", xytext=offset,
                fontsize=8, color="#52514e")

### The measured matched-parameter gap.
ax.annotate("", xy=(9.6, incumbent_val), xytext=(9.6, 0.005828),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="#0b0b0b", lw=1.2))
ax.text(10.6, 0.0037, "2.34×\nmeasured", fontsize=8.5, color="#0b0b0b")
ax.axvline(134, color="#898781", lw=1.0, ls="--")
ax.text(120, 0.0205, "parity by pure scaling\n~134M (global slope)\n~230M (local slope) ",
        fontsize=7.5, color="#898781", va="top", ha="right")

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.45, 420)
ax.set_ylim(0.0018, 0.022)
ax.set_yticks([0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02],
              ["0.002", "0.005", "0.010", "0.020"])
ax.minorticks_off()
ax.set_xlabel("trainable parameters (millions)")
ax.set_ylabel("DrivAerML validation relative $L^2$")
ax.grid(True, color="#e1e0d9", lw=0.8)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left", frameon=False)
for spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Placing GeoTransolver's matched-protocol anchor (0.00249 at ≈9.5M
params) on that curve:

- At GeoTransolver's own budget the gap is now **measured, not
  extrapolated: 0.005828 at 9.6M — a 2.34× gap at matched
  parameters** (the curve had predicted 2.5×). The rung fell
  inside its pre-registered band (@sec-nb-scalelaw: 0.0050–0.0061;
  falsifier ≥ 0.0070 refuted), toward the band's shallow end —
  which is the bend above showing up exactly where the
  pre-registration said it would matter.
- **Parity by pure scaling recedes as the frontier bends**: the
  global slope projects ~134M parameters; if the newest local slope
  (0.27) persists, ~230M. Still mostly-single-seed, width and depth
  moving together, the LR-constrained ×4 point excluded — but the
  budget-matched rung is now a measurement, and it telegraphs the
  trend. **Program decision: the pure-scaling ladder stops at
  ×2L8.** The next factor of 2 is sought in per-parameter
  architectural efficiency (the separable far-field decode and
  kernel structure), not another rung; ×2L8 becomes the working
  scale reference.

The interpretation is that scaling helps along a clean but bending frontier,
and GeoTransolver holds a **measured 2.34× per-parameter advantage
in-distribution**. The program's compensating assets are its
pre-registered bets — OOD generalization (next section, now under
the corrected vector metric), exact contracts, similarity
equivariance, zero-shot BC handling. Whether any of those is
*differential* rather than merely absolute was pre-registered as
the decisive comparison (@sec-nb-scalelaw-verdict), and the answer
turned out to be depth- and metric-dependent. **At zero-shot depth
the falsifier fired** (@sec-nb-geot-ood-zeroshot,
@sec-nb-corrected-zeroshot): under the corrected metric both
architectures degrade the same way (vector-WSS ~1.12× for each;
pressure ≤1.03 ours / ≤1.07 theirs) — no differential at the
boundary of the DoE hull, and the prediction that GeoTransolver
would degrade ≥1.5× was wrong. **At deep extremes a consistent
differential appeared** (@sec-nb-deep-differential): the OOD
section's paired exclusion-retrain comparison separates the
architectures on S1 with non-overlapping seed ranges — details
where the OOD evidence lives, below.

### The kernel factorial: the attribution verdict {#sec-drivaerml-factorial}

The external review's sharpest question was the one the industrial
program had skipped: is the exact boundary-integral structure — the
thesis mechanism — actually what carries the DrivAerML result? The
pre-registered test (@sec-nb-review,
@sec-nb-factorial-verdict-industrial): at the flagship rung, vary
ONLY the member dictionary, 1-node 500-epoch protocol, 3 seeds per
arm, against the flagship's own 3-seed control.

| arm | member dictionary | finals (3 seeds) | mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| flagship (control) | 2 exact + 8 learned | 0.0138 / 0.0140 / 0.0156 | 0.0145 |
| exact-only | 2 exact (0 params) | 0.0144 / 0.0138 / 0.0156 | 0.0146 |
| MLP-only | 8 learned, no exact | 0.0153 / 0.0151 / 0.0167 | 0.0157 |

**The pre-registered falsifier fired.** The prediction was
MLP-only ≥ 1.25× the flagship; the measurement is 1.084×, with
overlapping seed bands. At this rung the in-distribution result is
carried by the rest of the architecture — the trace formulation,
typed attention and moments, and capacity — so the accurate
description of the industrial model is **boundary-integral-inspired**.
Exact-kernel *causation* is established only where it was proven:
the synthetic program, whose ladders and margins stand unchanged.
The external review forced this test, and its skepticism was
substantially correct.

What remains is precise: exact-only beats
MLP-only on **every paired seed** (~7% each) — two closed-form,
zero-parameter members outperform eight learned ones at equal
non-member parameters — and exact-only is indistinguishable from
the flagship itself (0.0146 vs 0.0145), which makes the flagship's
eight learned members **evidence-orphaned at this rung**: the
simpler exact-only configuration is a parsimony candidate for the
default. The thesis's second barrel then fired the same way: the
**zero-shot OOD rider** (all six factorial checkpoints on the
never-seen S1/S2 splits, corrected vector metric,
@sec-nb-rider-verdict) measured *indistinguishable* degradation
ratios — MLP-only 1.11–1.14×, exact-only 1.11–1.13× — refuting the
prediction that exact far-field structure would matter more
off-distribution. **The exact-kernel demotion at this rung is
total**: neither in-distribution accuracy nor OOD robustness. The
exact dictionary's ~7% absolute edge does carry into OOD errors
(an accuracy offset, not a robustness slope), and one exploratory
counterpoint is on record: at the 9.6M ×2L8 rung, removing the
learned members costs ~9% (0.00635 vs 0.00583) — single seed
against a known ±12% rung spread, so the default configuration
keeps its members and the parsimony swap is not adopted.

### The trace factorial: the dominant mechanism, decomposed {#sec-drivaerml-trace-factorial}

If the exact kernels do not carry the industrial result, what does?
The trace factorial answers with the program's cleanest attribution
(@sec-nb-trace-factorial-verdict; pre-registered as review item 3's
decomposition, with the no-trace control added mid-campaign when
the kernel factorial demonstrated that effect sizes measured at
small configurations need not survive scale). Same protocol
discipline as every arm above: 1-node, 500 epochs, 3 seeds,
flagship capacity, one mechanism toggled at a time.

| arm | jump correction | trace readouts | finals (3 seeds) | mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no-trace | – | – | 0.0525 / 0.0524 / 0.0604 | 0.0551 |
| correction-only | ✓ | – | 0.0148 / 0.0153 / 0.0161 | 0.0154 |
| readouts-only | – | ✓ | 0.0149 / 0.0151 / 0.0162 | 0.0154 |
| flagship (both) | ✓ | ✓ | 0.0138 / 0.0140 / 0.0156 | 0.0145 |

Two findings, both structural:

1. **Trace is the dominant mechanism of the industrial program:
   3.8× at flagship capacity.** It *grew* from the 2.03× measured at
   the small pre-ladder configuration — the mirror image of the
   kernel members, whose effect compressed to noise at the same
   rung. Mechanisms scale individually; measuring each at the
   operating configuration is the only valid attribution. The
   ranking at flagship now reads: trace 3.8× ≫ capacity (the
   frontier's 2.4× from 0.6M→9.6M) ≫ member dictionary (0–8%).
2. **The two trace sub-mechanisms are near-perfect substitutes.**
   Correction-only and readouts-only land within 0.1% of each other,
   each recovering ~96% of the log-gap; enabling both adds a final
   ~6%. The mechanistic reading: the essential information is
   *boundary self-identification* — a channel telling the decoder
   that a query point IS the boundary at its own panel. The exact
   exterior jump constant (+½, zero parameters, licensed by the
   jump relation) and the learned own-cell readouts each deliver
   that bit; once either does, the other is largely redundant. The
   default keeps both (the 6% is free at inference); any future
   variant — including the separable far-field decode — must
   preserve at least one such channel, and the exact correction is
   the principled zero-parameter choice.

The two factorials together give the chapter its causal summary, and
it is worth seeing on one axis — because the ordering is the opposite
of what the program's thesis predicted.

```{python}
#| label: fig-attribution
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Industrial mechanism attribution, every factor measured at the SAME
#|   flagship operating point by a 3-seed pre-registered factorial that
#|   toggles one mechanism at a time. The trace formulation dominates;
#|   capacity is second; the exact singular dictionary -- the program's
#|   thesis mechanism -- contributes 0-8%. Hollow markers show where two
#|   mechanisms were measured at the SMALL pre-ladder configuration: the
#|   trace effect GREW with capacity (2.03x to 3.8x) while the member
#|   dictionary COMPRESSED to noise. Effect sizes are properties of an
#|   operating point, not of a mechanism. Values from this chapter's
#|   factorial tables; the synthetic-program causation (@sec-benchmarks)
#|   is unaffected -- there the exact members were varied on problems
#|   whose exact kernels are the right ones.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

### Flagship-capacity factorials, 3 seeds each (tables above).
no_trace, flagship = 0.0551, 0.0145        # trace factorial
mlp_only = 0.0157                          # kernel factorial
small_plain, small_trace = 0.1019, 0.0503  # pre-ladder trace anchors
small_plain_m, small_members = 0.1019, 0.0999
frontier_lo, frontier_hi = 0.0140, 0.005828  # 0.6M -> 9.6M rungs

mechanisms = [
    ("trace formulation\n(jump + self-identification)", no_trace / flagship,
     small_plain / small_trace, "#2a78d6"),
    ("capacity\n(0.6M → 9.6M params)", frontier_lo / frontier_hi, None, "#eda100"),
    ("exact singular dictionary\n(the thesis mechanism)", mlp_only / flagship,
     small_plain_m / small_members, "#e34948"),
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.0, 3.0))
for i, (label, factor, small, color) in enumerate(mechanisms):
    y = len(mechanisms) - 1 - i
    ax.plot([1.0, factor], [y, y], color=color, lw=7, solid_capstyle="butt",
            alpha=0.85, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(factor, y, "o", ms=10, color=color, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=4)
    ax.annotate(f"{factor:.2f}×", (factor, y), textcoords="offset points",
                xytext=(12, -3), fontsize=9.5, color="#52514e", fontweight="bold")
    if small is not None:
        ax.plot(small, y, "o", ms=9, mfc="none", mec=color, mew=1.8, zorder=5)
        ax.annotate(f"{small:.2f}× at small config", (small, y),
                    textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0, 11),
                    fontsize=7.5, color="#898781", ha="center")

ax.axvline(1.0, color="#0b0b0b", lw=1.0)
ax.text(1.02, 2.42, "no effect", fontsize=7.5, color="#0b0b0b")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(0.93, 5.4)
ax.set_xticks([1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5], ["1×", "1.5×", "2×", "3×", "4×", "5×"])
ax.minorticks_off()  # log minor labels otherwise leak past the explicit ticks
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, 2.75)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(mechanisms)),
              [m[0] for m in reversed(mechanisms)], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("validation-error factor gained (log scale)")
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#e1e0d9", lw=0.8)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
for spine in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Generalization: the OOD protocol and its verdict

This is the program's north-star axis — a surrogate that only
interpolates its training geometry is not an engineering tool — and
DrivAerML initially had no out-of-distribution evaluation. We
defined one, in the dataset's own generative coordinates: the
upstream design-of-experiments varies 16 shape parameters, and 483
of the 484 runs carry their official DoE values
(@sec-nb-ood-protocol). Two splits were adopted, each with a
leakage audit:

- **S2 — wake-topology corner** (primary): the joint top decile of
  backlight angle + rear-end tapering, **49 held-out cars** — the
  two-factor extreme that flips rear-wake topology. Median margin
  along the score direction ≈ 37× the training-set spacing.
- **S1 — ride-height double-extreme**: top and bottom deciles of
  ride height, **98 cars** — single-factor extrapolation in both
  directions on ground-effect physics.
- A third candidate (a neighborhood carve) was downgraded based on its geometry:
  a space-filling 16-D DoE leaves no interior holes (nearest-
  neighbor ratio 0.98×), so it tests nothing.

**Boundary read (zero-shot).** The standard-split flagship, evaluated
on the OOD cars it never saw — with the overlap made explicit: the
standard 435-car training set already contains 88/98 of S1 and 45/49
of S2, so the valid zero-shot sets are the never-seen remainder
(**n = 10 and 4**, at the *boundary* margin of the OOD regions),
against 36 never-seen in-distribution cars as the matched reference.
Degradation under the corrected vector metric
(@sec-nb-corrected-zeroshot, superseding the direction-blind
aggregate of @sec-nb-ood-zeroshot): **pressure 1.00–1.03×, but
vector WSS 1.12–1.13×** across three seeds — the WSS penalty is
real and resolvable above seed spread. The old metric compared
magnitudes only and had hidden the hardest part of the field:
for both this model and GeoTransolver, **WSS direction error is
~3× the magnitude error** (ours 0.72 vs 0.21 relative L2 at the ID
reference; GeoTransolver's 0.28 vs 0.09), and GeoTransolver's
zero-shot WSS ratios sit in the same band (1.12–1.16×).

**Deep read (OOD-trained).** The decisive version: retrain the
flagship on the OOD-train sets (385/434 cars; validation from a
carve of the same distribution, extremes untouched by selection),
then evaluate each run on its **full** held-out extreme set — 98/98
and 49/49 cars, three seeds per protocol, each run against its own
in-distribution reference so the smaller-training-set effect cancels
(@sec-nb-ood-deep-verdict):

All WSS figures below use the corrected joint-component vector
metric (@sec-nb-deep-differential; the direction-blind magnitude
figures of the original table survive in the notebook as
`wss_mag`). Ratios are each run's extremes against its own ID
reference:

| protocol | seed | ID ref (p / wss rel-L2) | extremes (p / wss) | degradation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 (n=98) | 42 | 0.195 / 0.779 | 0.198 / 0.845 | 1.02× / 1.09× |
| S1 | 43 | 0.176 / 0.721 | 0.181 / 0.783 | 1.03× / 1.09× |
| S1 | 44 | 0.226 / 0.919 | 0.233 / 0.985 | 1.03× / 1.07× |
| S2 (n=49) | 42 | 0.187 / 0.815 | 0.192 / 0.787 | 1.03× / 0.97× |
| S2 | 43 | 0.175 / 0.772 | 0.180 / 0.755 | 1.03× / 0.98× |
| S2 | 44 | 0.184 / 0.797 | 0.189 / 0.776 | 1.03× / 0.97× |

The pre-registered bars were ≤2× (S1) and ≤3× (S2); the measured
degradation is **pressure 1.02–1.03× everywhere, vector WSS
1.07–1.09× on S1 and none on S2** (slightly inverted — the
wake-topology corner does not stress WSS direction at all). The
excess degradation remains 11–100× smaller than the allowed excess.
Integrated drag concurs: 4.5–5.4% relative CD error in-distribution
vs 6–7% on the S1 extremes, 4–6% on both for S2.

**The differential — provisional at five seeds on WSS; pressure demoted.**
GeoTransolver's exclusion-retrain arms — same splits, harness,
metric, and protocol — give the paired comparison the zero-shot
read could not, now at five seeds per model
(@sec-nb-deep-differential, sealed in @sec-nb-seal-verdict):

| model | S1 press ratio | S1 wss ratio | S2 press | S2 wss |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| this program (5 seeds) | 1.019–1.044 | **1.072–1.113** | 1.03 | 0.97–0.98 |
| GeoTransolver (5 seeds) | 1.043–1.069 | **1.126–1.136** | 1.03–1.05 | 0.99 |

On S1 vector WSS the seed ranges are disjoint at 5-vs-5. The historical
independent rank-sum calculation gives $p \approx 0.008$, but it
discards the matched-seed design; with only five same-sign paired
differences, the minimum two-sided exact sign-test $p$ is 0.0625.
GeoTransolver's mean excess degradation is
1.4× ours (0.131 vs 0.092). The pre-registered extension narrowed
the estimate in both directions — the effect passed its no-overlap
test, but the original "ours ≤ 1.10" bound failed
(seeds 45/46 came in at 1.113/1.104), so the observed effect is
thinner than the 3-seed read suggested (1.4×, not 1.65×). On
pressure the extension ranges TOUCH (our 1.044 vs their 1.043):
per the same falsifier logic the pressure differential is demoted
to *suggestive* — consistent ordering of means (1.031 vs 1.056),
not seed-separated. Scope: the differential is in
generalization *ratios* — absolute errors still favor GeoTransolver
~2.5–2.7× everywhere (its capacity advantage), and both models sit
far inside the engineering bars.

*How to read this — and how not to.* Both caveats inline: the drag
figures are **pseudo-coefficients** (predicted and true fields
integrated on the same 10k-cell subsample — a valid error measure,
not comparable to full-mesh CD values); and the extremes are
**parameter-space extrapolation within the DrivAer family** — real
aerodynamic regime shifts (wake topology, ground effect), but not
novel vehicle topologies. Within that stated scope: **geometry
generalization on the industrial benchmark is observed at ~3% (pressure)
and ~8% (vector WSS, S1 only) degradation — boundary and deep, both
protocols. At deep-S1 its vector-WSS degradation ratio is consistently
smaller than GeoTransolver's at five seeds per side, but absolute WSS
errors favor GeoTransolver by 2.5–2.7× and the paired uncertainty is
too thin for “sealed” language. On pressure the five-seed extension
demoted the differential to *suggestive*: the ranges touch, the
means still order in our favour. One field remained consistent but
provisional; one softened — that is what the extension bought, in both
directions.**

And one boundary this whole section does not cross: every split above
is drawn from the DrivAer family's own design-of-experiments. The
next section leaves the family, and the result is categorically
different.

### Cross-family transfer: the decisive test, and the gauge it broke on {#sec-drivaerml-crossfamily}

Everything in the section above is *within-family* generalization:
the extremes are parameter-space extrapolation inside the DrivAer
notchback family. The program's stated identity — generalization
first — needs the harder version, and we pre-registered it
(@sec-nb-crossfamily-prereg): take DrivAerML-trained checkpoints and
evaluate them, with no retraining and no re-fitting of anything, on
**SHIFT-SUV** — a different vehicle family entirely. Same frozen
inference pipeline for every model, corrected vector metric, 20-case
estate pilot. The pre-registered falsifier was blunt: *if
GeoTransolver transfers equal or better, the generalization identity
fails its decisive test.*

**It fired beyond its own scale** (@sec-nb-crossfam-verdict).

| model | SHIFT pressure $L^2$ | SHIFT wss $L^2$ | own-family ID (p / wss) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| GeoTransolver anchor | **0.677** | 123.5 | 0.061 / 0.280 |
| MT flagship s42 | 1.3 × 10¹⁵ | 6.4 × 10¹⁷ | 0.167 / 0.705 |
| MT flagship s43 | 8.1 × 10⁴ | 5.1 × 10⁷ | 0.169 / 0.710 |
| MT flagship s44 | 4.1 × 10¹³ | 2.8 × 10¹⁴ | 0.180 / 0.737 |
| MT ×2L8 | NaN | NaN | 0.107 / 0.479 |

: Zero-shot cross-family transfer under the frozen (fixed-gauge)
protocol. GeoTransolver degrades ~11× on pressure and stays
structured; every MeshTransformer checkpoint — two capacities, three
seeds — diverges to non-physical output. {#tbl-crossfamily}

The result is solid in the way that matters: all four of our
checkpoints explode while GeoTransolver stays finite *through the
identical pipeline*, the fork's fairness audit verified
$L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ equality and the pressure/WSS sign conventions,
and the fresh ×2L8 own-family denominator (0.107 / 0.479) confirms
the checkpoints themselves are healthy. This is not a data artifact.
It is our model failing.

#### Localizing the mechanism

The failure *texture* — 10⁴ → 10¹³ → 10¹⁵ → NaN across seeds — is the
signature of an internal magnitude blow-up rather than a wrong-answer
regime, which points at the one number in the industrial pipeline
that is neither learned nor derived: the declared scale gauge. The
DrivAerML dataset config hard-codes `reference_length: 8.0`, chosen
years-equivalent ago to put the *wind tunnel* at a sane nondimensional
size (@sec-nb-drivaer-smoke). A constant with units of length,
calibrated to one family's absolute dimensions, is exactly the kind of
input the architecture's own gauge design exists to abolish
(@sec-intrinsic-gauge) — and the industrial arms took the licensed
override instead.

A single-checkpoint scan confirms it, cleanly and monotonically:

```{python}
#| label: fig-crossfamily
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Left: zero-shot cross-family transfer under the frozen protocol
#|   (fixed gauge 8.0). Every MeshTransformer checkpoint leaves the
#|   physical range by 5-16 orders of magnitude; GeoTransolver stays
#|   structured at 0.677. The shaded band is the models' own-family
#|   in-distribution error, i.e. where a transferring model would
#|   land. Right: the gauge dose-response on ONE checkpoint (flagship
#|   s42) with only the declared reference length varied. It is clean
#|   and monotone, which localizes the failure to the fixed gauge --
#|   but it is a test-set-touching scan and is therefore EXPLORATORY
#|   (hatched): it can name a mechanism, it cannot score a repair.
#|   Data: results/crossfamily_transfer_2026-07-22.json.

        "mt_flagship_seed44", "mt_x2L8"]

### The band a transferring model would land in: own-family ID errors.

id_hi = max(v1[k]["own_family_id_pressure_l2"] for k in keys)

top = 1e17
for i, (value, color) in enumerate(zip(values, colors)):
```

Gauge 8 → 1.3 × 10¹⁵; gauge 16 → 5.12 (finite, structured); gauge 48
→ 1.71. Three framings are all true at once, and the chapter keeps
all three:

1. **The frozen-protocol verdict stands as measured.** The deployed model
   does not transfer. The falsifier fired
   against the deployed protocol, and no diagnostic run afterwards
   un-fires it.
2. **The mechanism is a repairable protocol flaw, not deep
   architectural brittleness.** With a sane gauge the *same weights*
   produce structured cross-family predictions.
3. **The scan is test-set-touching and therefore exploratory.** No
   rehabilitated transfer claim may rest on it. Noted for calibration
   only: even the best exploratory gauge (1.71) is still ~2.5× worse
   than GeoTransolver's frozen-protocol transfer, so the realistic
   goal of a repaired re-run is "transfers comparably," not "wins."

#### The repair: an intrinsic gauge, calibrated once

The architecture already derives its gauge intrinsically by default —
the measure-weighted RMS boundary radius of @sec-forward-pass. What
the industrial pipeline needed was not a new mechanism but a way to
use that mechanism *while preserving the operating point every
existing checkpoint was trained at.* The repair
(@sec-nb-gauge-calib) is one dataset transform:

$$
L_{\mathrm{ref}}(\text{sample}) \;=\; C \cdot r_{\mathrm{RMS}}(\text{sample}),
\qquad
C \;=\; \frac{8.0}{\operatorname{mean}_{\text{train}} r_{\mathrm{RMS}}},
$$

with $r_{\mathrm{RMS}}$ the sample's own measure-weighted RMS radius
about its measure-weighted centroid — translation- and
rotation-invariant and similarity-*covariant*. The historical run
claimed Horvitz–Thompson subsample robustness and a calibration
performed **once on the DrivAerML training split**. The audit found both
claims invalid in the executed path: effective weights are stripped,
and the calibration iterated all 484 dataset cases rather than the
435-case training sampler. Its artifact reports
$r_{\mathrm{RMS}} = 0.30215 \pm 0.0089$ and hence
$C = 26.476593$, putting DrivAerML's per-sample gauges in
$[7.41, 8.64]$ — a ±3.5% spread around the historical 8.0, well
inside the measured stable zone. Any other family now operates at the
same *relative* operating point instead of inheriting DrivAerML's
absolute size.

Two acceptance gates were declared before either number existed
(@sec-nb-gauge-accept-verdict), and they split:

| lane (id_reference) | pressure $L^2$ | wss $L^2$ |
|---|--:|--:|
| flagship s42, fixed 8.0 | 0.167163 | 0.705265 |
| flagship s42, intrinsic | 0.178731 | 0.728916 |
| GeoTransolver, fixed dataset | 0.061000 | 0.279863 |
| GeoTransolver, intrinsic dataset | 0.061000 | 0.279863 |

: The paired acceptance evaluation. {#tbl-gauge-acceptance}

**Gate 2 (inertness) passes** — GeoTransolver declares no
`reference_length_key`, so it should be blind to the change, and its
digits are *identical* across dataset variants. That is the control
that makes the whole comparison interpretable: the variant YAML
changes the gauge and nothing else. **Gate 1 (drop-in preservation)
fails as pre-registered**: +6.9% pressure, +3.4% WSS against a 2%
bar. Since $\operatorname{mean}(C \cdot r_{\mathrm{RMS}}) = 8.0$ on
train by construction, the drift comes from the per-sample
*spread*, not an offset — the fixed-gauge checkpoint is more
gauge-sensitive than the coarse dose-response suggested. 6.9% is
sensitivity, not catastrophe; but the falsifier was written in
advance and it fired, so the pre-declared consequence stands: **the
intrinsic gauge is not a drop-in, and the confirmatory path is
retraining under it.**

#### Where this stands, and one anomaly worth more than the result

Three intrinsic-gauge retrains have finished (500 epochs, 1 node,
protocol otherwise identical to t2). Transfer-v2 is fully
pre-registered — gates, predictions, and the explicit list of
forbidden post-hoc moves — at @sec-nb-transfer-v2-prereg, and no
SHIFT-SUV number for any intrinsic-trained checkpoint exists yet.
The declared bars: all three seeds finite with pressure $L^2 < 1.0$
(structural, predicted $p \approx 0.75$), then seed-median
$\le 1.354$ for "transfers comparably" ($p \approx 0.45$) or
$\le 0.677$ for at-par ($p \approx 0.15$).

Before any of that, gate 0 asks the boring question — did the
retrained models stay as good in-family? — and the training curves
already flag something:

| seed | intrinsic-gauge training val | fixed-gauge training val |
|---|--:|--:|
| 42 | 0.01389 | 0.01383 |
| 43 | 0.01452 | 0.01404 |
| 44 | **0.03539** | 0.01561 |

: Intrinsic retrains against their fixed-gauge twins.
{#tbl-intrinsic-retrain}

Seeds 42 and 43 reproduce their twins almost exactly. **Seed 44
converged to a 2.3× worse basin.** The tempting reading — "seed 44 is
just unlucky" — is available for most of this program's tables, but
not this one: under the fixed gauge the three seeds were tight
(0.01383 / 0.01404 / 0.01561). The supported conclusion is that
**the intrinsic gauge introduced seed-dependent training instability
that the fixed gauge did not have**, and the divergence guard (train
loss > 10³) is not built to catch a soft 2.3× regression. Two
hypotheses stand: the per-sample gauge adds input-scale variance
that interacts badly with some initializations, or the gauge spread
widens learning-rate sensitivity until 3.0 × 10⁻³ is marginal. A
retrain of seed 44 at half the learning rate discriminates them
cheaply.

This is recorded here rather than smoothed away because it is the
more interesting object. A transfer result is one number about one
pair of datasets; a gauge that makes training seed-dependent is a
statement about the architecture's conditioning, and it would apply
to *every* future deployment that adopts the intrinsic gauge.

#### Transfer-v2: the repair was tested, and it failed {#sec-drivaerml-transferv2}

The confirmatory run is complete, and the repair does not work.

Six intrinsic-gauge checkpoints ran zero-shot on SHIFT-SUV through the
frozen pipeline. Four of them (seeds 42, 43, 45, 46) passed gate 0 — the
pre-registered in-family gate — and form the panel; seed 44 failed gate
0 at both learning rates and is reported beside them rather than
dropped.

| arm | SHIFT pressure $L^2$ | |
|---|--:|---|
| GeoTransolver anchor | **0.677** | the bar |
| s42 | 5.97 × 10³ | panel |
| s43 | 2.12 × 10¹⁰ | panel |
| s45 | 1.90 × 10¹³ | panel |
| s46 | 1.24 × 10⁷ | panel |
| s44 @ lr 3.0e-3 | **18.2** | gate-0 failure, reported |
| s44 @ lr 1.5e-3 | 2.33 × 10³ | gate-0 failure, reported |

: Transfer-v2. Gate 1 required every panel seed finite and below 1.0.
{#tbl-transferv2}

**Gate 1 fails.** Every seed is finite — a change from v1, which
produced a NaN — and every seed is three to thirteen orders of
magnitude past the bar. Gate 2 is moot. The pre-registered structural
prediction was $p \approx 0.75$; it was wrong.

This refutes the previous section's own diagnosis. The divergence was
initially attributed to the fixed gauge from a monotone but
test-set-touching dose-response and
described as "a repairable protocol flaw, not deep architectural
brittleness". Retraining under a similarity-covariant, per-sample
intrinsic gauge — using a constant mislabeled as train-only — leaves the
model diverging. **The gauge was an intervention that changed the magnitude,
not the cause.** What the earlier section got right was insisting the
dose-response was exploratory and could not support a rehabilitated
claim; that is why this is a clean refutation rather than a retraction.

*The excluded seed is the best transferrer.* Seed 44 — the worst
in-family model in the program — transfers two orders of magnitude
better than any panel seed, and its lower-learning-rate variant, which
trained *closer* to the healthy band, transfers *worse*. At $n = 6$
with thirteen orders of spread this is an observation and not a claim,
but it is the reason the gate-0 failure was reported rather than
dropped: **in-family fit and cross-family robustness may be in
tension**, and dropping the failing seed would have discarded the most
suggestive datum in the experiment while looking like good practice.

The consequence for the chapter's framing is direct. Three independent
probes — resolution (@sec-drivaerml-coverage), measure magnitude
(@sec-four-properties), and geometry family (here) — now support one
description: **the trained model is a regressor fitted to a narrow
operating point, and the exact-kernel structure does not protect it
outside that point.** That is consistent with the kernel factorial's
0–8% (@sec-drivaerml-factorial): structure that is not essential
in-distribution should not have been expected to carry generalization.
I now assign less than 5% probability to a cross-family *advantage* over the
GeoTransolver on the current mechanism; the
provisional within-family deep-S1 WSS degradation-ratio differential is
likely to remain this architecture's strongest industrial
generalization observation, subject to the metric and paired-uncertainty
audit above.

### The model is a coverage-specific regressor {#sec-drivaerml-coverage}

::: {.callout-warning title="What this sweep does and does not identify"}
The sweep below changes source and trace-query sets together, compares a
trained car model to an unrelated sphere estimator, and mixes an
approximately 8.8M pre-triangulation quad-dominant cell count with a
post-triangulation sampler. The curated reader documents roughly 17.7M
triangles in the cited case. Production selects a cyclic
contiguous block in on-disk cell order, whereas the sphere diagnostic
uses simple-random subsets. The U-shape is real; its
coverage-specific-correction mechanism and the grey quantitative comparison
are not identified. See @sec-program-review.
:::

Chapter @sec-future carries an item filed as *blocked on research, not
wiring*: at full resolution — 17.7M query cells against 50k sources —
the flagship's relative $L^2$ is $\sim$100, with no identified cause.
It now has a mechanism, contrary to the initial hypotheses.

The test is as simple as tests get: take one unchanged checkpoint
(flagship s42, the best-characterised in the program), evaluate it on
`id_reference`, and vary **nothing but `sampling_resolution`**.

```{python}
#| label: fig-coverage-cliff
#| fig-cap: >
#|   One unchanged checkpoint, one split, nothing varying but the source
#|   sampling resolution. The error has a sharp minimum exactly at the
#|   resolution the model was trained at (10k, dashed) and rises in BOTH
#|   directions -- catastrophically above it, reaching 24,811 at 40k. The
#|   10k lane reproduces the historical 0.167163 to six digits, so the
#|   sweep is clean. A model approximating a boundary integral better with
#|   more sources would fall monotonically; this is the signature of a
#|   fitted correction to one sampling rate. Grey: the pure-numerics
#|   sampling error of an EXACTLY evaluated boundary integral at the same
#|   coverages -- the model beats it at 10k, which is only possible
#|   because it is not approximating the integral at all. Data: AGA job
#|   293567; grey curve from studies/gauge_diagnostics/exact_rms.py.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

res = [2500, 5000, 10000, 20000, 40000]
err = [0.8966, 0.7998, 0.167163, 0.4106, 24810.9]
### Exact-estimator field-level relative L2 at the matching coverages
### Historical calculation used coverage = res / 8.8e6
### pre-triangulation cells, while the reader samples post-triangulation
### triangles; retained here as campaign history.
ex_res = [10000, 20000, 40000]
ex_err = [0.337, 0.248, 0.174]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.0))
ax.axvline(10000, color="#0b0b0b", lw=1.0, ls="--", zorder=1)
ax.text(10500, 3e3, "trained here", fontsize=8.5, color="#0b0b0b")
ax.plot(ex_res, ex_err, "s--", ms=6, lw=1.4, color="#898781", zorder=2,
        label="exact boundary integral (pure numerics)")
ax.plot(res, err, "o-", ms=9, lw=2.2, color="#e34948", mec="white", mew=1.2,
        zorder=4, label="trained MeshTransformer")
for r, e in zip(res, err):
    txt = f"{e:,.0f}" if e > 100 else f"{e:.3f}"
    ### The trained-resolution label goes left; below would collide with
    ### its own x tick.
    off, ha = ((-10, -4), "right") if r == 10000 else ((0, 13), "center")
    ax.annotate(txt, (r, e), textcoords="offset points", xytext=off, ha=ha,
                fontsize=8.5, color="#a83a39", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1800, 62000); ax.set_ylim(0.08, 2e5)
ax.set_xticks(res, [f"{r//1000}k" for r in res])
ax.minorticks_off()
ax.set_xlabel("source sampling resolution (historical pre-triangulation denominator)")
ax.set_ylabel("id_reference pressure relative $L^2$")
ax.grid(True, color="#e1e0d9", lw=0.8)
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper left", frameon=False)
for spine in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

| resolution | coverage | pressure $L^2$ | vs trained |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 500 | 0.028% | 0.8966 | 5.4× worse |
| 5 000 | 0.057% | 0.7998 | 4.8× worse |
| **10 000** | **0.11%** | **0.167163** | ← trained here |
| 20 000 | 0.23% | 0.4106 | 2.5× worse |
| 40 000 | 0.45% | **24 810.9** | **148 000× worse** |

: Resolution sweep on an unchanged checkpoint. {#tbl-coverage-cliff}

**Doubling the source count costs 2.5×; quadrupling it destroys the
model.** An operator that approximates a boundary integral gets *better*
with more sources. This gets catastrophically worse, and the minimum
sits exactly where training put it.

The grey curve is what makes the reading unambiguous. An *exactly*
evaluated boundary integral — exact singular kernels, no learning —
carries $\approx$34% field-level sampling error at 0.11% coverage
(@sec-four-properties). The trained model reads 0.167 there: **better
than the integral it is supposedly approximating.** A model cannot beat
its own quadrature by approximating it more accurately. It can only be
fitting coefficients that absorb the systematic part of the sampling
error *at one sampling rate* — which is precisely why the accuracy
evaporates when the rate moves.

**Where the failure lives.** Two candidate homes, and the measurements
separate them. At random initialisation the operator is well-behaved
under subsampling (∼9% at 1.6% coverage, converging); the *trained*
model is 148 000× wrong at 4× its training resolution. Both cannot be
properties of the architecture's quadrature, so **the pathology is in
the learned weights, not the operator** (@sec-nb-measnorm-caveat). A
gauge-based attempt to rescale the measure back to its training value
did not rescue it either — and its control showed why the intervention is
unusable: changing the gauge alone at fixed resolution costs 8×
(@sec-nb-measmech-verdict).

**Consequences for interpreting every DrivAerML number in this chapter.**

1. Every accuracy figure here is *at one coverage*, and is not evidence
   about the model at any other. The chapter's numbers are correct and
   internally comparable — every arm shares the protocol — but they do
   not transfer to deployment resolutions.
2. The full-resolution inference failure is no longer unexplained. It
   is this curve, one step further along.
3. It is a **protocol** pathology before it is an architectural one,
   which is good news: protocol is cheaper to change.

Two separable arms are in flight against it — one
architectural (`measure_normalization`, which removes a measure-magnitude
sensitivity the operator has) and one protocol
(`RandomCoverageSubsample`, which denies the model a single sampling
rate to overfit). Both are pre-registered with falsifiers
(@sec-nb-hca-launch); current evidence favors the protocol arm, and
neither is expected to touch the separate ~35% coverage-completeness
floor that no reweighting scheme reduces (@sec-four-properties).

### Decode efficiency: the 14× repricing

The archived profile that the cluster's idle-GPU telemetry forced found a
102k-launch dispatch storm in the
shared closed-forms path (an `einsum` lowering to a 4.2×10⁷-batch
bmm) and a bitwise member loop that was sequential by design. Both fixed —
the second under a physics-lined contract split: closed forms stay bitwise, learned members
move to measured-tolerance GEMMs with a bitwise reference mode
retained. Result: **7.2× (singpair) and 14.2× (members) step
speedups**, 474/474 tests, live on both clusters. Every wall-clock
number in this chapter is now ~an order of magnitude cheaper than
when it was measured.

The last decode economy is configuration, not code. The
checkpointed query-chunk decode — mandatory at B200 memory — costs
~10× on the 278-GB B300s, where the whole batched decode fits. The
paired same-seed control (@sec-nb-scalelaw-verdict) licenses
turning it off: ×2 rung, seed 42, chunked 0.0093 vs unchunked
0.00896 — **accuracy-neutral** (the 3.7% is inside the rung's seed
noise), so unchunked is the default for every rung from here. The
earlier unchunked outlier that raised the question (0.0114, seed
44) was seed variance, and is counted in the ±12% spread the scale
law's error bars carry.
